title: What the reformers asked
hook: grace, scripture, and real abuses; Catholics today admit many of the abuses were real

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Reformation began with a list for debate. Your line was a monk wanted reform. Today, what exactly did the reformers ask for? Day seven hundred eighty-two.

A papal envoy stands before a German assembly with a message from the new pope, Adrian the Sixth. The assembly may have expected a defense. Instead, the envoy reads out a confession. The pope's instruction admits that for years there had been grave abuses in the Holy See itself, that the sickness had spread from the head to the members, and that the pope means to begin the cure at home. A pope, in the middle of the storm, saying: some of this is our fault. Today's title is a question: what the reformers asked.
screen: `AN ENVOY, A CONFESSION.` → `FROM THE HEAD TO THE MEMBERS.` → `WHAT DID THEY ASK?`

segments.voice: The reformers asked three kinds of things. First, grace. Luther read Paul's letter to the Romans, which in the Douay-Rheims says, "The just man liveth by faith." He came to believe we are made right with God by grace, received through faith, not earned. Catholics also teach that grace comes first and can't be bought. The real disagreements were about how grace works in a person, and those took longer to sort out. Second, scripture. The reformers wanted the Bible in ordinary people's hands and languages, and they held it to be the final rule over every church teaching. Catholics hold scripture and tradition together, read within the Church. That disagreement is real, and it's still discussed. Third, the abuses. This is where the reformers were often simply right. Some bishops drew income from dioceses they rarely saw. Church offices were bought and sold. Some priests had barely been taught. And indulgences had been marketed like a product. Pope Adrian's instruction said as much. So did Catholic reformers inside the Church, before and after Luther. Then, why it matters. It's possible to disagree with the reformers about grace or scripture and still say plainly: they saw real wounds. The Second Vatican Council said that for the separations, often enough, people on both sides were to blame. Honest reform can start with that kind of admission: the abuses were real.
screen: `FIRST: GRACE, NOT EARNED.` · `SECOND: SCRIPTURE IN EVERY HAND.` · `THIRD: THE ABUSES.` · `HONESTY BEFORE REFORM.` · then, large: `THE ABUSES WERE REAL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name a reform you need. Not one someone else needs. One in you. Use the sit. Let your week pass before you: what you said, what you spent, how you treated the people closest to you. Somewhere there's a habit that's drifted, the way an office drifts into a privilege. Don't fix it yet. Just name it, plainly, the way Pope Adrian's letter named the abuses. One sentence, said honestly to yourself. If you pray, you can bring that sentence before God. The bell holds the time.
Luther. The reformer who read Paul on grace, called for scripture in everyone's hands, and pointed to abuses the Church needed to face. Today's word.
Your line: the abuses were real. Today, when someone criticizes something you love, listen first for the part that's true before you defend the rest. Day seven hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Catholic and Protestant theologians continue to discuss grace, scripture and authority in formal dialogues; Catholic leaders have publicly acknowledged that abuses in the Church of that era were real.

fork.setup: you're a new pope. a reform movement is tearing the West apart, and some of its complaints about Rome are true. what do you send?
options: a flat denial of every charge.
an admission that the sickness began at the head, and a promise to cure it at home.
fork.reveal: Adrian VI's instruction admitted grave abuses in the Holy See and said the cure would begin there.

trapdoor: what you thought: the reformers just wanted to leave the Church.
what it means: they asked about grace, about scripture, and about real abuses, and on the abuses they were often right.
what a scholar hears: Adrian VI's instruction to his legate, admitting the corruption had spread from the head to the members.
recall: honor, a bow, a kiss, a candle

sources.quoted: The just man liveth by faith.

sources.ref: Instruction of Adrian VI to the legate Chieregati, Diet of Nuremberg

notes: Adrian VI's instruction to Francesco Chieregati, read at the Diet of Nuremberg (1522–23), paraphrased: 'for some years many abominations... in this Holy See', 'the sickness has spread from the head to the members'. Confirm wording and that the envoy read it out.
The three kinds of request (grace, scripture, abuses) follow the index hook; the summary of each side is simplified. Confirm fairness to Lutheran and Reformed positions.
Examples of abuses (pluralism of benefices, simony, poorly taught clergy, marketed indulgences): confirm.
'Catholic reformers inside the Church, before and after Luther': confirm acceptable without names.
'Catholic leaders today say so': general claim per the index hook; Keeper may prefer a specific citation.
The index word is the title head 'What the reformers asked', kept exactly.

Editor: softened uncited 'several dioceses... lived in none' and 'many priests'; replaced the unsourced 'Catholic leaders today say so' with a paraphrase of Unitatis Redintegratio 3 (added to sources); toned down the overclaim that honesty 'was the starting point' of reform.
Editor 2: 'Everyone expects a defense' softened (no claim about the assembly's minds); varied the teach's closing line.
Audit: 'pardon had been marketed' changed to 'indulgences had been marketed' (an indulgence is not a pardon of sin); 'often enough' restored from Unitatis Redintegratio 3.
